phonemes.desc: Open unrounded vowel [a], the first syllable of the Avestan name.
Long [aː], the stem vowel held and resonant.
Short [h] plus [i], the middle syllable carrying the stress in the restored form.
Long final [aː], the feminine ending that completes the divine name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-NAH-hee-tah' — the stress settles on the penultimate syllable, and the final vowel is drawn out.

kin.label: Middle Persian / Parthian
kin.form: Anāhīd / Anāhīt, the form preserved under the Sasanians and in Zoroastrian Middle Persian

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Uncertain; often derived from Avestan ānāhitā, "undefiled, immaculate"

pronunciation.note: Anāhitā is Tier 1 because the restored form preserves distinctive length and the macron-bearing ā, features the ASCII form anahita flattens entirely.

domains.title: The Immaculate Waters
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Healing, and Wisdom
domains.lead: Anāhitā is the great Yazata of the Avestan pantheon, the goddess of the life-giving waters, and one of the most widely worshipped deities of ancient Iran. She is called Aredvi Sura Anāhitā — the moist, strong, undefiled — and her realm runs from the mythical river that surrounds the world to the springs that nourish fields, wombs, and kings.

cards.name: Lady of the Waters
cards.desc: The Avestan Yasht 5 hymns her as the source of all rivers, the force that makes the cosmos fertile and clean.

cards.name: Fertility and Royalty
cards.desc: Kings pray to her for legitimacy, warriors for victory, women for safe childbirth, and farmers for abundant crops.

cards.name: Star of the Waters
cards.desc: She is linked to the planet Venus in later tradition — the bright star that rises from and governs the waters.

cards.name: Golden Splendor
cards.desc: The hymn describes her clothing of gold, her crown, her earrings, and her necklaces — a figure of Iranian royal magnificence.

symbols.name: Running water
symbols.meaning: The river, spring, or canal that is her body and her blessing

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: The flower that rises from the water, a later emblem of her purity and fertility

symbols.name: Star (Venus)
symbols.meaning: The celestial body identified with Anāhitā in Sasanian and later Zoroastrian tradition

symbols.name: Golden dress and crown
symbols.meaning: The royal insignia described in Yasht 5, marking her as patron of legitimate kingship

mythology.lead: Anāhitā's mythology is concentrated in the fifth Yasht of the Avesta, a long liturgical hymn that praises her powers and lists the kings and heroes who sacrificed to her.

myths.title: The Hymn to the Waters
myths.text: Aredvi Sura Anāhitā is praised as the mighty river that flows from Mount Hara into the sea Vourukaša, feeding the seven rivers of the earth. The Yasht asks her to come down from the stars to receive sacrifice, and it promises her worshippers fertile fields, healthy children, victorious armies, and long life. She is simultaneously a cosmic geography and a personal savior.

myths.title: Royal Patroness
myths.text: Artaxerxes II and later Achaemenid kings invoked Anāhitā in their inscriptions alongside Ahura Mazdā and Mithra. Her cult spread through the empire, and temples were erected to her at Ecbatana, Susa, and Babylon. For the Iranian aristocracy, devotion to Anāhitā was a marker of loyalty and legitimacy.

myths.title: Lady of the Lakes
myths.text: Under the Sasanians, Anāhitā was identified with the planet Venus and worshipped at major fire-temples and lake-sanctuaries. Lake Hāmūn in Sīstān and the Ādur-Anāhīd fire at Stakhr were centers of her cult. Armenian sources preserve the memory of her temples and processions, where horses and chariots were dedicated to her.

lore.syncretism: Anāhitā absorbed and was absorbed by neighboring goddesses. In Armenia she was identified with the indigenous goddess Nana or Nanē, and with the Greek Artemis and Tyche. The Seleucid and Parthian periods saw her portrayed in Hellenistic dress with a mural crown, tympanum, and lions — the visual vocabulary of the Syrian goddess Atargatis. Some scholars compare her functions to those of the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna and the Indic Sarasvatī, though these are typological parallels, not direct borrowings. She is best understood as an Iranian development of the ancient Near Eastern goddess of water, fertility, and sovereignty.
lore.culturalLegacy: Anāhitā's name lived on in Iranian languages as Anāhīd, a popular female name and a poetic word for the planet Venus. The pre-Islamic Iranian new year, Nawrōz, preserved water-rituals that honored her. In modern Zoroastrian practice, the veneration of water and the divine feminine continues, and Anāhitā remains one of the best-known Yazatas outside the tradition. Her temples at Kangāvar and Bīšāpūr are among the most impressive surviving monuments of Sasanian religion. Restoring Anāhitā recovers the long vowels and stress that distinguish the Avestan goddess from the flattened modern name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Anāhitā is the water that knows no stain. In a religious world dominated by fire and light, she represents the sacred power of moisture, fertility, and the female divine. Her name means undefiled, and her cult asks human beings to keep the waters clean — an ecological commandment older than any modern environmentalism.

She is also a royal goddess, the patron of legitimate rule, and her hymn is a catalogue of the great who sought her favor. To meditate on Anāhitā is to meditate on the waters that make civilization possible: the river, the spring, the canal, the womb. She asks not for war but for purity, not for conquest but for the careful tending of life.

lore.archaeology: Major temples dedicated to Anāhitā have been identified at Kangāvar (often identified with the temple of Artemis/Anāhitā mentioned by Isidore of Charax), Bīšāpūr, and Takht-e Soleymān. Sasanian and Kushano-Sasanian coinage depicts her with mural crown, lotus, and lions. Achaemenid inscriptions from Susa and Hamadan name her alongside Ahura Mazdā and Mithra, confirming her place in the official cult of the empire.
